rv.q: This life-affirming show proves that and more – an absolute tonic.
This is a brilliant addition, in the optimum venue, to the West End landscape.
The sweet script achieves a delicate balance between humour, lightness and some more painful recollections.
For all its sorrow, the play gleams with hope.
It’s a unique show with the texture of theatre but the communal immediacy of stand-up.
If attitudes towards talking about mental health have moved on in the past ten years then that is only a good thing, even if some of the show’s messages feel slightly pat today.
But there’s something about the scale and downright snazziness of this production that doesn’t quite gel.
Every Brilliant Thing is in its totality endearing but today risks feeling pathologically non-specific, like an Ed Sheeran song about heartbreak or a straight-to-Netflix movie about being alive.
Yet the problem is as much with Henry as the shallow script.
But to me, with its scripted improvisation, it often felt mawkish and shallow.
In its decision to balance grief and glee and not to allow one to exclude the other, this is a clear-sighted, heartening show.
A beautiful and heartfelt piece of theatre, with sincerity and without sentimentality.
Even with its unpromising title, this really is a remarkable piece of work despite being crafted from the same loathsome material as the average West End musical: sentimentality.
It will send most people home joyful rather than brooding.
As a collective, participatory experience, it’s really quite brilliant.
He teases, flirts, dances, never missing a beat or breaking a sweat.
It’s clearly an incredibly moving device for most, but for a small minority, the writing is overly sentimental and simplistic and rather akin to a public service announcement for adolescents.
Artistically, it’s as demanding as listening to a knock-knock joke or reading the contents on a cereal box.
As brilliant as it is possible for one show to be.
This may just be the play of the year.
Donahoe’s return is a triumph, and Every Brilliant Thing remains one of the most vital and life-affirming shows you’ll ever see.
Every Brilliant Thing is a salve to the challenges of our global society and a heartfelt call for thoughtful conversation and compassionate understanding for one another.
Every Brilliant Thing defies expectations and its unique concept creates a rare moment of connection among the audience.
It feels instead like finding something long lost and unexpectedly precious.
On the other hand, the simplicity of the story, the clarity and openness of its feelings, does make this a very moving experience, as well as one full of laughter.
Right now, though, this West End staging is all about the audience participation and interactions, to which Henry is no stranger.

cn.t: This acclaimed interactive solo show about depression finally reaches the West End to mostly warm reviews. Critics praise its emotional resonance and audience participation, though some find it manipulative or overly reliant on performer charisma.
